screens.title: Network Security with Security Groups, NACLs, & AWS WAF
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how three AWS controls work together to protect your network: Security Groups, Network Access Control Lists, and AWS WAF. Security Groups act as stateful, instance-level firewalls. NACLs provide stateless, subnet-level filtering with explicit allow or deny rules. AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic at the application layer and can block attacks before they reach your origin. You will see concrete examples: opening HTTP to a web server, blocking that same traffic at the subnet level with a NACL deny, and how WAF applies rule sets to stop malicious requests. This chapter emphasizes practical decisions: use NACLs for broad subnet protections or to immediately block bad IP ranges, use Security Groups for fine-grained instance access, and use WAF to defend web applications against common exploits and abusive request patterns. As you go through the screens, notice common pitfalls—like making Security Groups too permissive or forgetting that NACLs are stateless—and understand the simple strategies that reduce risk. By the end you should be ready to design a layered, durable network security posture and test it safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these exercises you'll be able to distinguish when to use Security Groups versus NACLs, configure Security Group rules safely, implement subnet-level NACLs and understand their stateless behavior, and apply AWS WAF rules to protect web traffic. Specifically, you'll learn to craft least-privilege Security Group rules and avoid broad SSH or all-traffic ingress. You will practice adding NACL deny rules with rule precedence so you can block malicious ranges across an entire subnet. You'll also get hands-on experience installing a web server, observing how a permissive Security Group can be blocked by a NACL, and then restoring traffic by adding matching outbound ephemeral port rules to the NACL. These are practical operator skills: configuring controls, testing behavior, and interpreting results. As you work, keep the guiding principle in mind: layered defenses reduce single-point failures. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember when to apply each control and how to verify it.

screens.title: Security Groups — Instance-level, stateful firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: Security Groups are virtual firewalls that you attach to compute and resource endpoints such as EC2 instances, load balancers, and RDS. The defining characteristic is statefulness: when a connection is allowed inbound, the return traffic is automatically permitted without an explicit outbound rule for that connection. You define rules as inbound or outbound and only specify ALLOW rules; anything not allowed is implicitly denied. A common example is allowing HTTP and HTTPS to a web server by adding inbound TCP rules for ports 80 and 443 from any IP address or a narrower CIDR if you need restricted access. Another frequent example is allowing SSH only from your office IP address. A frequent mistake is making SGs too permissive, for instance allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. That exposes your instance to scanning and brute force attempts. Because instances can have multiple Security Groups attached, you can split responsibilities: one SG for SSH from admin networks and another SG for web traffic. Key practice: keep SG rules minimal, prefer specific source CIDRs or other Security Groups, and name rules clearly so reviewers can quickly understand intent. Question for you: when would you prefer referencing another Security Group as a source instead of an IP range?

keyIdea.title: Security Group rule principle
keyIdea.text: Stateful, allow-only rules attached to instances; minimize scope and prefer group-to-group references when possible.

content.html:
Core Concept
Definition & best practices
What a Security Group is

A stateful, instance-level virtual firewall that holds ALLOW rules for inbound and outbound traffic. Return traffic matching an established connection is automatically permitted.

Example
Allow inbound TCP 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 to serve a public website.
Common mistake
Allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 exposes instances to the internet; prefer a single admin IP or a VPN CIDR.
Key Takeaway

Use Security Groups for precise, stateful access control to individual resources and keep rules least-privilege.

How rules look (conceptual)
# Inbound rules
Allow TCP 22 from 203.0.113.5/32   # SSH from admin IP
Allow TCP 80  from 0.0.0.0/0        # HTTP public
Allow TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0        # HTTPS public

# Outbound rules (often permissive)
Allow All traffic to 0.0.0.0/0
Tip: split duties across multiple Security Groups so auditing and least-privilege reviews are simpler.
Check your understanding
Why does allowing inbound HTTP require no explicit return rule? Because SGs are stateful and automatically allow response traffic for established connections.

screens.title: Network ACLs — Subnet-level, stateless filters
screens.narratorSegment: Network Access Control Lists, or NACLs, are stateless filters applied to subnets. They differ from Security Groups in several key ways: they work at the subnet boundary rather than the instance, they are stateless so return traffic must be explicitly allowed, and they support both ALLOW and DENY rules evaluated in ascending rule-number order. A simple, practical use is quickly blocking a malicious IP range across every resource in a subnet by adding a low-numbered DENY rule for that CIDR. Because NACLs evaluate rules by number, the first matching rule determines the outcome. New NACLs default to allowing all traffic, so when you add restrictive rules you must verify both inbound and outbound rules to accommodate return traffic. For example, if you allow inbound HTTP (port 80), you also need an outbound rule that permits ephemeral ports for responses. Misconception to avoid: NACL DENY rules only affect the subnet, not instance-level groupings, and they do not automatically open return traffic. Takeaway: use NACLs for coarse, fast blocking across subnets, and always mirror required return rules due to statelessness. Network ACLs — Subnet-level, stateless filters means stateless, ordered allow and deny rules at subnet level; must include matching return rules for successful connections.. In practical terms, how nacls apply ordered allow/deny rules at the subnet boundary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Stateless, ordered allow and deny rules at subnet level; must include matching return rules for successful connections.

content.html:
Definition
Subnet boundary filtering
What a NACL is

A stateless ACL for a subnet that evaluates ordered ALLOW or DENY rules. The first matching rule by number applies to the traffic.

Example
Add a low-numbered inbound DENY for 192.0.2.0/24 to block a malicious range across the entire subnet.
Stateless behavior
If you ALLOW inbound port 80, you must ALLOW outbound ephemeral ports for return traffic.
NACL rule list (conceptual)
Rule 100: Deny 0.0.0.0/0 TCP 22-22   # block SSH from everywhere
Rule 110: Allow 0.0.0.0/0 TCP 80-80  # allow HTTP
Rule 120: Allow 0.0.0.0/0 TCP 1024-65535 # allow ephemeral outbound for responses
Remember: ordering matters. A low-numbered DENY can override later ALLOWs and immediately protect the subnet.
Key Takeaway

Use NACLs for broad subnet policies and fast, precedence-based blocking; always add corresponding return rules because they are stateless.

screens.title: Testing interactions: SG allow vs NACL deny
screens.narratorSegment: Testing how Security Groups and NACLs interact exposes real operational behavior. A common test sequence is: first, create an EC2 instance with a Security Group that allows HTTP and SSH, confirm the web server responds, then add a low-numbered inbound DENY for HTTP to the subnet's NACL and observe that the web server stops responding. This demonstrates that NACLs act at the subnet boundary and can block traffic that an SG allows. Next, remove the DENY and replace it with an ALLOW for HTTP, and add an outbound ALLOW for ephemeral ports on the NACL to permit return traffic; after this change the web server returns to working. This step-by-step process concretely shows statelessness: inbound and outbound rules are separate. Misconception check: if you only add an inbound ALLOW to NACL but forget outbound ephemeral permits, the connection may still fail. Practice this controlled sequence to build intuition and to verify your rules when you troubleshoot connectivity issues. Testing interactions: SG allow vs NACL deny means launch instance, allow at sg, deny at nacl to block, then add matching nacl outbound to restore—this proves statelessness and precedence.. In practical terms, a practical sequence that reveals precedence and stateless behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test sequence
keyIdea.text: Launch instance, allow at SG, deny at NACL to block, then add matching NACL outbound to restore—this proves statelessness and precedence.

content.html:
Process Flow
Step-by-step validation
1
Launch instance & allow HTTP in SG
Confirm a web page loads using the instance public IP. This verifies the SG allow path is functioning.
2
Add low-numbered inbound DENY on NACL for HTTP
Reload the web page and observe it fails. This shows the NACL can block traffic that the SG permits.
3
Replace DENY with ALLOW and add outbound ephemeral rule
After adding both inbound HTTP ALLOW and outbound ephemeral ALLOW, test again and expect success because the NACL now permits return traffic.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm SG inbound rule for the service port exists.
  • Check NACL inbound rule numbers and whether DENY exists earlier.
  • Add outbound ephemeral range 1024-65535 to NACL when allowing inbound services.
  • Use browser or curl to test behavior after each change.
Key Takeaway

A NACL deny overrides an SG allow at the subnet edge; restoring service requires both inbound and outbound NACL rules because NACLs are stateless.

screens.title: Security Groups vs NACLs — Side-by-side
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Security Groups and NACLs side-by-side clarifies when to use each. Scope: SGs attach to instances and are fine-grained; NACLs attach to subnets and affect all resources in that subnet. Statefulness: SGs are stateful, so return traffic is automatic; NACLs are stateless, requiring explicit inbound and outbound rules. Rule types: SGs only express ALLOW rules with implicit deny otherwise; NACLs support ALLOW and DENY explicitly with ordered evaluation by rule number. Default behaviors differ as well: default SGs typically deny inbound and allow outbound, while default NACLs allow all until you change them. Application: use SGs to limit which ports and sources can reach a particular instance or load balancer; use NACLs for coarse-grained protections like blocking an IP range across a subnet. Misconception: choosing both is redundant — in practice they complement each other. Use NACLs for broad boundary policies and SGs for resource-level, least-privilege controls. Remember: an instance can have multiple SGs, but each subnet has one active NACL association. Security Groups vs NACLs — Side-by-side means sgs: stateful, instance-level, allow-only. nacls: stateless, subnet-level, ordered allow/deny.. In practical terms, compare scope, statefulness, rule types, and evaluation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Clear contrasts for design decisions
Security Groups
  • Instance-level scope
  • Stateful: return traffic auto-allowed
  • Only ALLOW rules; implicit deny
  • Multiple SGs per instance possible
Use case
Fine-grained access control to services and ports on specific resources.
Network ACLs (NACLs)
  • Subnet-level scope
  • Stateless: explicit return rules required
  • ALLOW and DENY rules with ordered evaluation
  • One NACL association per subnet
Use case
Coarse-grained blocking or filtering across an entire subnet, like blocking a malicious CIDR.

screens.title: AWS WAF — Application-layer protection
screens.narratorSegment: AWS WAF operates at the application layer to inspect HTTP and HTTPS requests. It protects web applications and APIs against common threats that lower-level filters cannot easily detect, such as S Q L injection patterns, cross-site scripting, or malformed payloads. You attach WAF using a Web ACL to CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, A P I Gateway, or AppSync. Rules within a Web ACL can match on IP addresses, request headers, URI strings, request body, size constraints, geographic origin, and rate-based thresholds. Managed rule groups provide pre-built protection that addresses known patterns and the OWASP Top 10; they reduce the operational burden of writing every rule yourself. Use-case example: deploy WAF on CloudFront to filter malicious requests globally and benefit from caching while blocking attacks before they reach your origin. Misconception: WAF is not a replacement for SGs or NACLs; it complements them by handling application-specific threats that network filters cannot examine. Core takeaway: add WAF when your application must inspect request content or rate patterns and use managed rules to cover common threats quickly. AWS WAF — Application-layer protection means waf inspects http/s at the application edge and applies web acl rules and managed rule groups to block web exploits and abusive traffic.. In practical terms, inspect and filter http/s requests with web acls and rule groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: WAF principle
keyIdea.text: WAF inspects HTTP/S at the application edge and applies Web ACL rules and managed rule groups to block web exploits and abusive traffic.

content.html:
Core Concept
Application-layer defense
What WAF does

WAF inspects HTTP/S requests with Web ACLs composed of rules that allow, block, or count requests based on IPs, headers, URIs, body content, size, geography, and rate.

Example
Use a rate-based rule to block IPs that make too many requests in a short time window to mitigate basic DDoS patterns.
Managed rule groups
Deploy pre-configured protections to cover common vulnerabilities without authoring every rule yourself.
Deployment targets
  • CloudFront — global, earliest filtering
  • Application Load Balancer — regional app edge
  • API Gateway / AppSync — API protection
Key Takeaway

Add WAF when you need content-aware protections and use managed rules for fast coverage of common web threats.

screens.title: Designing a layered network security strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A robust network security design uses multiple layers: NACLs at the subnet boundary for coarse filters, Security Groups for precise instance protection, and AWS WAF for application-layer inspection and rule enforcement. Start with NACLs that block known bad ranges or restrict traffic between tiers, for example preventing direct access from the public web to database subnets. Next, assign Security Groups that only open necessary ports per instance — web servers get 80 and 443, database servers accept traffic only from application-tier SGs. Finally, place WAF in front of public HTTP/S endpoints via CloudFront or an ALB to block injection attempts, malicious headers, or abusive request rates. Architecture
Layered defenses for resilience
Typical layered pattern
Boundary: NACL
Block broad malicious CIDRs and restrict cross-tier traffic at the subnet level.
Resource: Security Groups

Edge: AWS WAF
Inspect HTTP/S traffic and stop content-level attacks and abusive rates.

Design with clear boundaries and small rule sets at each layer so policies are easier to review and incidents are isolated quickly.

Naming, audits, and reviews
Naming and descriptions

screens.title: Managed Rule Groups and WAF lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Managed rule groups are pre-configured WAF protections provided by AWS or marketplace sellers that cover common web threats and known vulnerability classes. They are useful because they reduce the need to author every rule and can be updated by the provider as new threats appear. When you adopt managed rules, tune them in counting mode first to observe what they would block, then move to blocking once you have confidence they don't cause false positives. This staged approach avoids accidentally denying valid traffic. Use managed groups as a baseline and add a small set of custom rules for application-specific needs. Misconception to avoid: managed rules are plug-and-play without impact — they can block legitimate traffic if not tested. Best practice: start in monitor mode, analyze counts, add exclusions for known safe patterns, then enable enforcement. This lifecycle reduces maintenance while preserving protection against evolving threats. Managed Rule Groups and WAF lifecycle means start in monitor/count mode, analyze hits, tune rules, then enable blocking to avoid false positives while maintaining protection.. WAF managed rules lifecycle
Why use managed rule groups
They provide curated protections for common vulnerabilities and reduce the operational burden of writing and updating many rules manually.
Staged approach
Monitor first, tune with exclusions, then enable enforcement.

Augment managed rules with a small set of application-specific checks.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core ideas front of mind. First, Security Groups are stateful, instance-level allow-only firewalls; they are the primary place to implement least-privilege access to an instance. Second, NACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that evaluate ordered ALLOW and DENY rules; they are ideal for broad, precedence-based blocking such as immediately denying a malicious CIDR across a subnet. Third, AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS at the application layer using Web ACLs and managed rule groups to stop content or request-pattern attacks. These three controls complement one another: NACLs set broad boundaries, Security Groups enforce resource-level policies, and WAF protects content and request patterns. When designing, document rules, test changes step-by-step, and adopt a monitor-then-enforce lifecycle for managed WAF rules to avoid false positives. Asking a simple verification question after each change—what test will prove this rule did what I expect—keeps your environment safer and easier to manage.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how three AWS controls work together to protect your network: Security Groups, Network Access Control Lists, and AWS WAF. Security Groups act as stateful, instance-level firewalls. NACLs provide stateless, subnet-level filtering with explicit allow or deny rules. AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic at the application layer and can block attacks before they reach your origin. You will see concrete examples: opening HTTP to a web server, blocking that same traffic at the subnet level with a NACL deny, and how WAF applies rule sets to stop malicious requests. This chapter emphasizes practical decisions: use NACLs for broad subnet protections or to immediately block bad IP ranges, use Security Groups for fine-grained instance access, and use WAF to defend web applications against common exploits and abusive request patterns. As you go through the screens, notice common pitfalls—like making Security Groups too permissive or forgetting that NACLs are stateless—and understand the simple strategies that reduce risk. By the end you should be ready to design a layered, durable network security posture and test it safely.

By the end of these exercises you'll be able to distinguish when to use Security Groups versus NACLs, configure Security Group rules safely, implement subnet-level NACLs and understand their stateless behavior, and apply AWS WAF rules to protect web traffic. Specifically, you'll learn to craft least-privilege Security Group rules and avoid broad SSH or all-traffic ingress. You will practice adding NACL deny rules with rule precedence so you can block malicious ranges across an entire subnet. You'll also get hands-on experience installing a web server, observing how a permissive Security Group can be blocked by a NACL, and then restoring traffic by adding matching outbound ephemeral port rules to the NACL. These are practical operator skills: configuring controls, testing behavior, and interpreting results. As you work, keep the guiding principle in mind: layered defenses reduce single-point failures. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember when to apply each control and how to verify it.

These additional objectives emphasize practical testing and layered design. You'll launch an EC2 instance, install a web server, and observe how Security Group permissions interact with subnet NACLs. You'll add a NACL DENY rule to see how it overrides an SG allow, and then add matching outbound ephemeral port rules to restore traffic, demonstrating statelessness. You will also learn to design a multi-layered strategy that places coarse filters at subnet boundaries, fine-grained rules at the instance level, and WAF at the application edge for HTTP traffic. Finally, you'll adopt an operational practice: regularly review and update your rules and consider managed WAF rule groups to reduce maintenance. These skills make your deployments safer in production and faster to troubleshoot when something blocks traffic unexpectedly. Each objective includes a simple visual clue to help you remember test patterns and verification steps.

Security Groups are virtual firewalls that you attach to compute and resource endpoints such as EC2 instances, load balancers, and RDS. The defining characteristic is statefulness: when a connection is allowed inbound, the return traffic is automatically permitted without an explicit outbound rule for that connection. You define rules as inbound or outbound and only specify ALLOW rules; anything not allowed is implicitly denied. A common example is allowing HTTP and HTTPS to a web server by adding inbound TCP rules for ports 80 and 443 from any IP address or a narrower CIDR if you need restricted access. Another frequent example is allowing SSH only from your office IP address. A frequent mistake is making SGs too permissive, for instance allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0. That exposes your instance to scanning and brute force attempts. Because instances can have multiple Security Groups attached, you can split responsibilities: one SG for SSH from admin networks and another SG for web traffic. Key practice: keep SG rules minimal, prefer specific source CIDRs or other Security Groups, and name rules clearly so reviewers can quickly understand intent. Question for you: when would you prefer referencing another Security Group as a source instead of an IP range?

Network Access Control Lists, or NACLs, are stateless filters applied to subnets. They differ from Security Groups in several key ways: they work at the subnet boundary rather than the instance, they are stateless so return traffic must be explicitly allowed, and they support both ALLOW and DENY rules evaluated in ascending rule-number order. A simple, practical use is quickly blocking a malicious IP range across every resource in a subnet by adding a low-numbered DENY rule for that CIDR. Because NACLs evaluate rules by number, the first matching rule determines the outcome. New NACLs default to allowing all traffic, so when you add restrictive rules you must verify both inbound and outbound rules to accommodate return traffic. For example, if you allow inbound HTTP (port 80), you also need an outbound rule that permits ephemeral ports for responses. Misconception to avoid: NACL DENY rules only affect the subnet, not instance-level groupings, and they do not automatically open return traffic. Takeaway: use NACLs for coarse, fast blocking across subnets, and always mirror required return rules due to statelessness. Network ACLs — Subnet-level, stateless filters means stateless, ordered allow and deny rules at subnet level; must include matching return rules for successful connections.. In practical terms, how nacls apply ordered allow/deny rules at the subnet boundary. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing how Security Groups and NACLs interact exposes real operational behavior. A common test sequence is: first, create an EC2 instance with a Security Group that allows HTTP and SSH, confirm the web server responds, then add a low-numbered inbound DENY for HTTP to the subnet's NACL and observe that the web server stops responding. This demonstrates that NACLs act at the subnet boundary and can block traffic that an SG allows. Next, remove the DENY and replace it with an ALLOW for HTTP, and add an outbound ALLOW for ephemeral ports on the NACL to permit return traffic; after this change the web server returns to working. This step-by-step process concretely shows statelessness: inbound and outbound rules are separate. Misconception check: if you only add an inbound ALLOW to NACL but forget outbound ephemeral permits, the connection may still fail. Practice this controlled sequence to build intuition and to verify your rules when you troubleshoot connectivity issues. Testing interactions: SG allow vs NACL deny means launch instance, allow at sg, deny at nacl to block, then add matching nacl outbound to restore—this proves statelessness and precedence.. In practical terms, a practical sequence that reveals precedence and stateless behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparing Security Groups and NACLs side-by-side clarifies when to use each. Scope: SGs attach to instances and are fine-grained; NACLs attach to subnets and affect all resources in that subnet. Statefulness: SGs are stateful, so return traffic is automatic; NACLs are stateless, requiring explicit inbound and outbound rules. Rule types: SGs only express ALLOW rules with implicit deny otherwise; NACLs support ALLOW and DENY explicitly with ordered evaluation by rule number. Default behaviors differ as well: default SGs typically deny inbound and allow outbound, while default NACLs allow all until you change them. Application: use SGs to limit which ports and sources can reach a particular instance or load balancer; use NACLs for coarse-grained protections like blocking an IP range across a subnet. A robust network security design uses multiple layers: NACLs at the subnet boundary for coarse filters, Security Groups for precise instance protection, and AWS WAF for application-layer inspection and rule enforcement. Start with NACLs that block known bad ranges or restrict traffic between tiers, for example preventing direct access from the public web to database subnets. Next, assign Security Groups that only open necessary ports per instance — web servers get 80 and 443, database servers accept traffic only from application-tier SGs. Finally, place WAF in front of public HTTP/S endpoints via CloudFront or an ALB to block injection attempts, malicious headers, or abusive request rates. This placement means even if a SG is misconfigured, WAF can stop many HTTP-based attacks before they reach the instance. Misconception: these layers are not redundant; they are complementary. NACLs provide fast, broad protection; SGs provide least-privilege controls; WAF protects content and request patterns. Keep three core ideas front of mind. First, Security Groups are stateful, instance-level allow-only firewalls; they are the primary place to implement least-privilege access to an instance. Second, NACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that evaluate ordered ALLOW and DENY rules; they are ideal for broad, precedence-based blocking such as immediately denying a malicious CIDR across a subnet. Third, AWS WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS at the application layer using Web ACLs and managed rule groups to stop content or request-pattern attacks. These three controls complement one another: NACLs set broad boundaries, Security Groups enforce resource-level policies, and WAF protects content and request patterns. When designing, document rules, test changes step-by-step, and adopt a monitor-then-enforce lifecycle for managed WAF rules to avoid false positives. Asking a simple verification question after each change—what test will prove this rule did what I expect—keeps your environment safer and easier to manage.

Second, remember NACLs are stateless and rule-number order matters; when you change NACL rules, think about both inbound and outbound directions to keep connections working. Third, use WAF to inspect and block application-layer attacks and start with managed rules in monitor mode to tune before enforcing. These reminders are practical checks you can run quickly when designing or troubleshooting: inspect SG source CIDRs, verify NACL outbound ephemeral permissions when enabling inbound services, and review WAF counts before switching to block.
